claims.text: The precursor is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy blend.
The precursor contains metallic powders and TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 hydrides.
The initial oxygen content is approximately 500-1000 ppm.
The precursor blend contains 5 wt% CaH2 getter powder.
CaH2 activation at approximately 800-900°C overlaps the TaH0.5 decomposition window.
A 900°C hold for 2 hours after heating at 2°C/min will facilitate sequential hydride decomposition and oxygen scavenging.
Heating to 1250°C at 10°C/min and holding for 30 minutes will homogenize the alloy.
CaH2 decomposes into Ca and H2.
Calcium subsequently reacts with oxygen to form CaO and scavenge oxygen.
The CaH2 getter will reduce oxygen partial pressure below 10^-15 atm.
A transient CaO layer forms on the surfaces of hydride particles.
Lower oxygen activity inhibits nucleation of alpha-HCP Ti/Zr-rich phases.
Lower oxygen activity stabilizes the high-temperature beta-BCC lattice.
Quenching faster than 100°C/s suppresses the diffusion-controlled transformation from beta-BCC to alpha-BCC plus beta-BCC.
Rapid quenching will retain a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure.
The processed alloy will exceed 98% of theoretical density.
The rapidly quenched alloy will have a grain size of 10-20 micrometers.
No detectable alpha-HCP phase or alpha-Ti precipitates will remain after quenching.
Sintering without a reactive getter or with Ti powder leaves more than 200 ppm residual oxygen and produces brittle alpha-Ti precipitates even after quenching.
The hypothesis is falsified by alpha-HCP or alpha-Ti peak intensity above 0.5% during 800-1000°C or by alpha-phase peaks after quenching.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says CaH2 decomposes to CaO while releasing hydrogen, whereas the mechanism says CaH2 first decomposes to Ca and H2 and CaO forms only through subsequent calcium oxidation.

The label 'alpha' is used inconsistently for alpha-HCP Ti/Zr-rich phases, alpha-Ti precipitates, and an asserted alpha-BCC phase, making the proposed transformation sequence and the phase that oxygen is claimed to stabilize ambiguous.
